title: The lost discipline of dream interpretation
gist: Pre-industrial societies slept in two segmented phases with a waking interval devoted to reflecting on dreams, a pattern that artificial lighting (from Edison's lightbulb onward) largely erased in favour of consolidated monophasic sleep, severing what historian A. Roger Ekirch calls humanity's oldest path to the psyche.

insights.claim: For most of human history, night-time sleep was divided into a 'first sleep' (roughly 9pm to midnight) and a 'second sleep' after dawn, with the intervening hours given over to bathing, socialising, praying and meditating.
insights.speaker: Garima Garg
insights.so_what: Establishes the historical baseline sleep pattern that modern monophasic sleep replaced, framing the article's core causal claim about artificial light.
insights.quote: The first sleep started around nine in the evening and lasted till midnight. For the next couple of hours, people bathed, socialised, prayed and meditated.

insights.claim: In modern sleep science terms, the pre-modern 'first sleep' corresponds to NREM sleep and the 'second sleep' corresponds to REM sleep, the phase associated with vivid dreaming.
insights.speaker: Garima Garg
insights.so_what: Reframes a historical/religious phenomenon (medieval monks' 'demonic' night wakings) in modern neuroscience terms, useful shorthand for the sleep-science angle on pre-modern practices.
insights.quote: In modern medical terms, the ‘first sleep’ is the NREM (Non-Rapid Eye Movement) sleep, simply the body’s daily biological reset. The ‘second sleep’ is what is known as REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep, characterised by rich and vivid dreams.

insights.claim: By the 12th century, the Church had institutionalised confession, forcing priests to contend with 'sinful' dreams; by the 1600s, dream interpretation itself was considered heretical.
insights.speaker: Garima Garg
insights.so_what: Traces the institutional/religious mechanism by which dream interpretation shifted from an accepted practice to a suppressed one, prior to the later technological disruption from artificial light.
insights.quote: By the 1600s, dream interpretation was even seen as ‘heretical’.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Whether they have believed themselves to be channelling God'

themes.theme: Artificial light as the cause of the shift to monophasic sleep

insights.claim: The author identifies Thomas Edison's invention of the lightbulb at the end of the 19th century as the key driver of the shift away from biphasic sleep, as artificial light became the dominant reality of the hours once given over to the first sleep, eventually producing a monophasic pattern of six-to-eight-hour continuous sleep.
insights.speaker: Garima Garg
insights.so_what: A clear causal claim linking a specific technology (electric lighting) to a fundamental change in human biological/cultural behaviour — a useful case study for how infrastructure technologies reshape ostensibly 'natural' human patterns.
insights.quote: When Thomas Edison invented the lightbulb at the end of the 19th century, artificial light became the dominant reality of the hours that constituted the first sleep.
insights.locator: Paragraph on the Church institutionalising confession

insights.claim: In a 1992 experiment, psychiatrist Thomas Wehr placed a group of people in darkness for about 14 hours a day; after a month, their sleep patterns reverted to the pre-modern biphasic pattern.
insights.speaker: Garima Garg
insights.so_what: Empirical evidence that biphasic sleep is a latent default human pattern suppressed by modern lighting conditions rather than a lost trait, supporting the causal claim about artificial light.
insights.quote: In 1992, a psychiatrist named Thomas Wehr conducted an experiment in which he placed a group of people in darkness for about 14 hours every day
insights.locator: Paragraph on the treasured eight-hour sleep cycle

insights.claim: Historian A. Roger Ekirch argues that the shift to consolidated monophasic sleep caused people to lose touch with their dreams and, with it, a traditional avenue to their deepest emotions, calling this 'the greatest loss' from modern lighting technology.
insights.speaker: Garima Garg
insights.so_what: The article's strongest interpretive claim: technological convenience (lighting) came with an under-recognised psychological cost, a framing applicable more broadly to trade-offs from other modern conveniences.
insights.quote: It is no small irony that, by turning night into day, modern technology has helped to obstruct our oldest path to the human psyche. That, very likely, has been the greatest loss

themes.theme: Dreams as foundational to consciousness, not cognitive residue

insights.claim: Sleep scientist Matthew Walker argues in 'Why We Sleep' that sleep, not wakefulness, was the first state of life on the planet, and that wakefulness itself emerged from sleep — implying modern society's mechanisation of sleep has also mechanised waking consciousness.
insights.speaker: Garima Garg
insights.so_what: Offers a scientific reframing that elevates dreaming/sleep from a secondary bodily function to a primary driver of consciousness, supporting the article's broader argument that something valuable was lost in the shift to monophasic sleep.
insights.quote: sleep was the first state of life on this planet, and it was from sleep that wakefulness emerged

insights.claim: The author concludes that while a return to biphasic sleep is unlikely, the mystical power of pre-modern dreamtime may not be lost so much as obscured, and could be re-investigated with renewed interest.
insights.speaker: Garima Garg
insights.so_what: The article's closing, exploratory suggestion — a soft opening for renewed cultural/wellness interest in dream interpretation practices rather than a strong prediction.
insights.quote: We may just discover that the mystical power of dreamtime has not been lost, only obscured.
